rv.q: “Hate Radio,” in contrast, was too disorienting to hiss at.
His work is not uncontroversial — which may be to the purpose.
What lingers is less a portrait of monstrosity than of normalcy.
It would be harrowing stuff if it wasn’t presented in the style of a dusty video exhibit playing on repeat in a forgotten corner of a museum.

In an age when media ecosystems amplify grievance, reward outrage, and cloak dehumanization in the language of patriotism or entertainment, Rau’s reconstruction feels less like historical reenactment than a diagnosis.
It’s haunting how normal their messaging may sound even as they are calling for the deaths of hundreds of thousands.
Shakespeare in New York continues to suffer from unnecessary tampering by directors desperate to make a mark.

cn.t: Critics praise Milo Rau's powerful docudrama for its chilling reconstruction of the 1994 Rwandan genocide's radio broadcasts, commending its haunting examination of language's dangerous power and its urgent warnings about propaganda's role in violence.

vr.q: It's a tough one, but I found it very insightful.
